A.explanation: This is the useful output power of the pump alone, $2.5 \text{ kW}$, before allowing for the $70\%$ efficiency to find the power supplied by the engine.

B.explanation: This is the input power to the pump, equal to the engine useful output: pump output $2.45 \text{ kW}$ divided by $0.70$ gives about $3.5 \text{ kW}$.

C.explanation: This is the gravitational potential energy gained, about $150000 \text{ J}$, with the $1.0$ minute time of $60 \text{ s}$ omitted so energy is mistaken for power.

D.explanation: This divides the energy of about $150000 \text{ J}$ by $0.70$ but still omits division by the $60 \text{ s}$ time, giving power far too large.

hints: Notice the $0.50 \text{ m}^3$ volume, $1000 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$ density and $30 \text{ m}$ lift - first find the mass lifted and its gain in gravitational potential energy $mgh$.
Recall that power is energy divided by time, so divide that $mgh$ energy by $1.0$ minute $= 60 \text{ s}$ to get the pump useful output power.
Connect the $70\%$ pump efficiency to the engine: efficiency $=$ useful output / input, so the engine must supply a larger input power equal to pump output divided by $0.70$.
walkthrough: Find the mass of water from density and volume: $m = \rho V = 1000 \times 0.50 = 500 \text{ kg}$.
Find the useful work done lifting it $30 \text{ m}$: $W = mgh = 500 \times 9.81 \times 30 = 147150 \text{ J}$.
Find the useful output power of the pump using the time $t = 1.0 \text{ minute} = 60 \text{ s}$: $P_{pump} = W/t = 147150/60 \approx 2450 \text{ W} \approx 2.5 \text{ kW}$.
Use pump efficiency $= 0.70 = P_{useful}/P_{input}$ to find the power the pump must be supplied: $P_{input} = P_{pump}/0.70 \approx 2450/0.70 \approx 3500 \text{ W}$.
That input power is the useful output power from the engine driving the pump, about $3.5 \text{ kW}$. This is option B.
